First home in Brampton? You may be able to claim up to $4,000 back.

Ontario's land transfer tax refund for eligible first-time buyers is up to $4,000. You must be at least 18, a Canadian citizen or permanent resident, and never have owned a home anywhere in the world, and you must move in within nine months of closing. Ask your lawyer how to claim it.
Source: Ontario.ca (Land Transfer Tax Refunds for First-Time Homebuyers, updated Feb 10, 2026). Eligibility rules apply.

Cambridge buyer: pay your mortgage every two weeks instead of monthly? Years off? Here is the math.

Example only, Canadian semi-annual compounding, $700,000 home, 20% down, 25-year amortization, 4.44% for the whole term:
1) A $560,000 mortgage costs about $3,081 a month.
2) Accelerated biweekly is half of that, about $1,540 every two weeks.
3) 26 payments a year equals one extra monthly mortgage payment, about $3,081 a year.
4) Result: about 3.3 years sooner and about $54,800 less interest, if the rate stayed the same. Rates usually change at renewal.
Source for the example rate: lowest 5-year fixed rate shown on Ratehub.ca, updated Nov 10, 2026. Ask your lender whether accelerated biweekly is offered.

Want help working out your own budget? Comment INFO to get full details, or call 905-452-4298.

Example only. Not mortgage, tax or legal advice.

Budget 2026 changed its homebuilding goal. What could it mean for buyers?

The Canadian Press reports (Nov 10, 2026) that Budget 2026 dropped the 2025 platform goal of doubling home construction, while the Housing Minister's office says the government is still working toward doubling homebuilding over the next decade. CMHC's baseline forecast, as cited by The Canadian Press, is about 231,000 homes built a year, which could leave a shortfall of up to 238,000 homes by 2036.

My take: supply is only one factor. Rates, prices and your own area's inventory matter too, so look at local sold prices and listings before you decide.

caption:
Milton buyers: you may not need 20% down.

The minimum down payment in Canada is 5% of the first $500,000 of the price plus 10% of the part from $500,000 up to $1.5 million (20% at $1.5 million or more). On a $700,000 home that is $25,000 + $20,000 = $45,000, compared with $140,000 for 20%. With less than 20% down you will typically need mortgage loan insurance, which adds a cost, and your lender still checks your income, credit and the home.
Source: Financial Consumer Agency of Canada (canada.ca). Confirm with your lender.

Want help planning your budget? Comment INFO to get full details, or call 905-452-4298.

General information only. Not mortgage advice.

frames.say: Milton: you may not need twenty percent.

Next, add ten percent of whatever part falls between five hundred thousand and one point five million.
Now the twist. Then, on a seven hundred thousand dollar home, that works out to forty-five thousand dollars, not one hundred forty thousand.
Finally, with less than twenty percent down you'll typically need mortgage loan insurance, and your lender still checks your income and credit.
